text: Starting with the first of the traits mentioned earlier, I will say that it is good to have a reputation for being generous. However, if you practice generosity in a way that goes unnoticed, it will actually harm you. If you are honestly generous, as you should be, it might not be recognized. Then you will not escape the reputation of being a miser. Therefore, anyone who wants to keep a reputation for generosity must put on a lavish display. A prince who does this will consume all his wealth in extravagant acts. In the end, to keep up his generous reputation, he will be forced to burden his people, tax them heavily, and do whatever it takes to get more money. This will quickly make his subjects hate him. As he becomes poor, no one will respect him. His generosity will have offended many and rewarded only a few. He will be vulnerable to the very first sign of trouble and endangered by the slightest risk. When he realizes this and tries to cut back, he will immediately be labeled a miser.

Therefore, a prince cannot safely practice the virtue of generosity in a way that people recognize, unless he is willing to ruin himself. If he is wise, he should not fear being called cheap. Over time, people will consider him more generous than if he had actually been generous from the start. They will see that his economy keeps his revenues sufficient. They will see that he can defend himself against attacks and undertake campaigns without burdening his people. Thus, he ends up being generous to the countless people he does not tax, and stingy only to the few people he does not give to.

In our time, we have only seen great things accomplished by those who were considered cheap. Everyone else has failed. Pope Julius the Second used his reputation for generosity to reach the papacy, but he did not try to keep it up once he declared war on the King of France. He fought many wars without imposing any special taxes on his subjects, covering his extra expenses through his long history of thriftiness. The current King of Spain would not have undertaken or won so many campaigns if he had a reputation for being generous. Therefore, a prince should not care about being called cheap, as long as it means he does not have to rob his subjects, can defend himself, does not become poor and pathetic, and is not forced to become greedy. Being cheap is simply one of the vices that allows him to rule.

Someone might argue that Julius Caesar obtained his empire through generosity, and many others have reached the highest positions because they were generous and had a reputation for it. I answer this: You are either already a prince, or you are on your way to becoming one. If you are already a prince, generosity is dangerous. If you are on your way to becoming one, a reputation for generosity is absolutely necessary. Caesar was one of those who wanted to become the supreme ruler in Rome. But if he had survived after reaching power and failed to cut his expenses, he would have destroyed his own government. Someone else might reply that there have been many princes who led armies and did great things, yet were considered very generous. To this, I reply that a prince either spends his own money, his subjects' money, or the money of others. In the first two cases, he must be thrifty. In the third case, he should take every chance to be generous. For a prince who leads his army and supports it by looting, sacking, and extortion, handling the wealth of others, this generosity is strictly required. Otherwise, his soldiers would not follow him. You can afford to be a generous giver of what belongs to neither you nor your subjects, just like Cyrus, Caesar, and Alexander. Squandering the wealth of others does not hurt your reputation; it only adds to it. It is only squandering your own wealth that hurts you.

Nothing consumes itself faster than generosity. Even as you practice it, you lose the ability to keep doing it. You become either poor and despised, or, in an effort to avoid poverty, you become greedy and hated. Above all else, a prince must protect himself from being despised and hated, and generosity leads directly to both. Therefore, it is wiser to accept a reputation for being cheap. It brings a bad name, but no hatred. This is far better than seeking a reputation for generosity, only to be forced into a reputation for greed, which brings both a bad name and intense hatred.
